# Wattever

> LLM endpoint throughput and deterministic task-accuracy benchmarking with optional local telemetry, public model configuration identities and shareable audit JSON. The Python helper supports managed LM Studio or externally managed streaming Chat Completions. Hosted browser timing uses a separate protocol; its capability catalog is read-only.

## README.md

Canonical source: [README.md](README.md)

# Wattever

Wattever benchmarks LLM endpoints across prompt sizes, models and simultaneous query counts, and compares successes and failures in a browser UI. Connect the local Python helper or hosted browser to an OpenAI-compatible streaming Chat Completions endpoint, including Strata, llama.cpp and LM Studio. The helper also offers managed LM Studio model loading and optional local GPU power measurements. Wattever uses Python 3.9+, the Python standard library and local JavaScript without a package installation or CDN.

## Browser quick start

Open [Wattever on GitHub Pages](https://lpalbou.github.io/Wattever/), start an OpenAI-compatible server, enable its CORS support, and use **Connect** to select models and run tests. Browser and server permissions can affect access to a local endpoint. See [Browser mode](docs/browser.md) for settings, storage, privacy and measurement limits.

## Full local helper quick start

1. Start your inference engine and load a model. For managed LM Studio operation, install LM Studio, download models and run `lms bootstrap` once. Other endpoints do not need LM Studio.
2. Clone the repository for the endpoint helper features described here. The [v2.4.1 source archive](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/releases/tag/v2.4.1) documents that historical release and predates these helper features.
3. On Windows run `Wattever.bat`; on macOS run `Wattever.command`; on Linux run `sh Wattever.sh`. Alternatively run `python -m wattever.server` from the repository.
4. Open the displayed local URL. On **Run**, choose **OpenAI-compatible endpoint**, enter your API base URL and use **Connect / discover models**. Wattever identifies the endpoint where evidence is available and supplies its display name automatically; no manual label or ID is required. Enter a model ID manually if discovery is unavailable. Choose workloads and start. Leave the server running until the benchmark finishes.

See [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) for both provider modes and [Measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md) for interpretation. The inference engine controls model quantization, context, KV cache and speculative decoding. GPU monitoring selects a sensor only. Generic endpoint power measurements require an explicit assertion that inference runs on the benchmark computer; remote inference power remains unavailable.

**Results** provides Summary, Table and Compare views with common benchmark, model, measure and concurrency filters. Tables can be copied as tab-separated text. Managed LM Studio runs support **Add / rerun tests**; generic endpoints use new runs. One JSON file stores each benchmark. Optional reproducibility settings and sourced compute claims accompany detected hardware without being presented as detected measurements. Review JSON before publication; see [results guidance](results/README.md).

The hosted Results view also includes a shared catalog that you can browse without connecting a model provider. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) to contribute your benchmark or add missing tests later.

## Capability tests and live telemetry

The helper's **Capabilities** tab runs original Core tasks, the pinned 1,319-question GSM8K test split, or the 1,172-question ARC-Challenge test split. Choose a deterministic subset or the full suite and compare auditable rule-scored answers. These are zero-shot chat adaptations, not official leaderboard scores or intelligence rankings. Requested reasoning, reported MTP/quantization and unknown effective settings remain distinct in public model/endpoint configuration fingerprints. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md) for scoring, dataset licenses and uncertainty.

Its visual dashboard combines strict pass rate, correct/planned and coverage tiles with category bars, an outcome ring and repeat comparisons. Select a chart to filter the paginated question-by-repeat matrix, then open a cell to inspect the question, expected output, model response and rule explanation. Matching evaluation protocols support paired comparisons that exclude unscored requests. A format mismatch or request error is shown distinctly from a passed answer; inspect the evidence before drawing conclusions about reasoning.

Local runs can display CPU/GPU utilization, RAM/VRAM usage, available temperatures, GPU clocks and power. Saved telemetry includes a bounded recent history and whole-run observed means/peaks/coverage; early/late changes are observations, not a throttling diagnosis. Results charts separate selected metrics into individual graphs. The hosted site can browse/export/compare shared capability results; launching tests and validating capability imports require the helper.

## docs/getting-started.md

Canonical source: [docs/getting-started.md](docs/getting-started.md)

# Getting started

For hosted use without installing Wattever, see [Browser mode](docs/browser.md). The instructions below cover the full local helper.

Install Python 3.9 or newer. Wattever does not need Python packages or a JavaScript build. Choose a provider mode:

- **OpenAI-compatible endpoint:** start an inference engine such as Strata, llama.cpp or LM Studio and load your model there. Wattever needs streaming Chat Completions; model discovery is optional. Other OpenAI API surfaces are not required or implemented by this integration.
- **LM Studio (managed):** install [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/), download models and run `lms bootstrap`. Wattever can load/unload models and schedule context and MTP settings through its CLI. The API defaults to `http://localhost:1234`; `LMS_BASE_URL` changes that managed connection.

Clone the repository for the generic endpoint helper features. The [v2.4.1 archive](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/releases/tag/v2.4.1) remains available with that release's feature set. Start `Wattever.bat` on Windows, `Wattever.command` on macOS, or `sh Wattever.sh` on Linux. You can also run `python -m wattever.server` in the repository. The server listens on loopback and prints its URL; keep its window open. `GPU_BENCH_PORT` sets the starting port (default 8713); `GPU_BENCH_NO_BROWSER=1` suppresses automatic browser opening.

On **Run**, choose your provider. For a generic endpoint, enter your engine's API base URL, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1` (a root URL also works), and optionally the name of an API-key environment variable. Set the variable before starting the helper; enter its name, never its secret value, in Wattever. Click **Connect / discover models**. Wattever supplies a display name and an opaque route identity automatically; no label or ID is required. If the provider does not expose `/models`, supply its exact served model ID manually. The Python helper connects directly, so browser CORS permission is only needed in hosted browser mode.

Endpoint names come from recognized public cloud hosts or explicit service metadata when available. Local/private metadata probes are bounded, read-only requests; Wattever does not identify software from a port number or model name. If the software cannot be established, it uses an honest **Local endpoint**, **Private endpoint** or **Remote endpoint** fallback. An optional advanced **Display name** override is the only naming field you need to edit. Detected route location does not establish where inference runs; the local-inference confirmation remains a separate assertion.

Select models, prompt sizes, query counts and repeats. Configure quantization, context allocation, KV cache, placement and MTP in the external engine. **Requested reasoning** defaults to **None** in the UI and sends `reasoning_effort`; choose **Provider default** to omit it. Unsupported values fail visibly, and accepted requests do not verify effective behavior. Reproducibility fields and reported MTP/reasoning record operator knowledge; they do not change the engine. A canonical model ID can identify a checkpoint behind a served alias. Each generic endpoint experiment starts a new run; load/unload, resume and same-file extension are available only for managed LM Studio.

Hardware discovery describes the benchmark client. Leave **I confirm inference runs on this computer** unchecked for remote or uncertain deployments. Checking it explicitly attributes local sensors to inference; it does not verify the server's hardware. The GPU selector chooses a power sensor, not execution placement. Record placement and other relevant settings, and close competing workloads for comparisons. The macOS launcher offers optional authorization for `powermetrics`; throughput measurements work without it.

Use **Results** to select and compare benchmark files, download JSON, or copy tables. See [measurements](docs/measurements.md) before comparing and [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) if setup fails. Return to [overview](README.md); see [API](docs/api.md) for integration.

Use **Capabilities** for task accuracy after connecting in **Run**. Select a model, suite and question count, review the answer budget and timeout, then start. Full suites can be lengthy; subsets record their exact seeded selection. Capability tests and validated imports require the helper. The hosted site supports their shared result library/export/comparison. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

After updating Python or UI files, restart the helper and reload its page to use the complete build. The launcher identifies builds with `/api/version` `build_id`, reuses the same build, and can replace an identified idle older build even when the release version is unchanged. Active speed or capability runs are preserved. Use the printed helper URL; its port is separate from your model server's port, and restarting Wattever does not require stopping the inference engine.

---

## docs/browser.md

Canonical source: [docs/browser.md](docs/browser.md)

# Browser mode

Open [Wattever on GitHub Pages](https://lpalbou.github.io/Wattever/) to run a quick benchmark without installing Wattever. Start LM Studio or another OpenAI-compatible server with models available. Enter its endpoint (the default is `http://localhost:1234/v1`) and select **Connect**; Wattever does not request the model list until you connect. Choose models and workloads, start the benchmark, and keep the page open until it finishes.

The provider must permit cross-origin requests. LM Studio has an Enable CORS switch in its [server settings](https://lmstudio.ai/docs/developer/core/server/settings). Browsers may also require local-network permission, and HTTPS-to-localhost behavior depends on the browser and its security settings; see [Microsoft Edge local network access](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/ms-edge-local-network-access). Wattever connects directly from the browser: it has no hosted proxy and does not use helper credentials. If the endpoint needs an API key, enter it in the page; the key stays in memory and the input clears after connecting. It is not saved in result files or browser storage.

Endpoint names and route IDs are automatic. Recognized official cloud hosts or explicit service metadata can identify the service; otherwise a Local/Private/Remote endpoint fallback is used. No manual label or ID is required, and an advanced **Display name** override is optional. Canonical known public API routes use stable public provider IDs; other routes, including custom cloud paths, use a private URL-to-random-ID mapping in browser local storage. That mapping is excluded from exports; clearing storage can regenerate its IDs. Detection describes the route/provider, not verified inference hardware or backend weights.

Chrome versions with separate network permissions may call localhost access **Apps on device** or **Loopback network**. Allow the permission for the Wattever site when you connect. The permission is distinct from access to other devices on your LAN; see [Chrome local network guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/local-network-access.md).

GPU, CPU, RAM and VRAM fields are optional user-supplied descriptions, not hardware discovery. Browser mode cannot measure GPU power or VRAM use, load/unload models, choose placement, allocate context, control MTP, resume a session or extend the same file. It can request standard reasoning effort, temperature and the supported token-limit field; the engine's effective behavior remains unverified. Unsupported request values fail visibly. Configure model execution in the provider. Use the [local helper](docs/getting-started.md) for detected client hardware and optional local telemetry; its managed LM Studio provider additionally supports lifecycle/context controls and same-file extension.

New browser results record `measurement_mode: browser`, `browser_schema_version: 2` and protocol `browser-2`, with bundled corpus identity and a SHA-256 hash when available. Timing includes network/browser overhead and is not directly comparable to helper protocols. Exact provider usage is required for token throughput; missing counts remain unavailable, with no character/chunk token estimate. Reasoning usage and observed output boundaries are recorded: reported unstreamed reasoning is excluded from decode, ambiguous hidden reasoning or a single output event leaves decode unavailable. Prompt tokens/client TTFT remains a proxy including possible hidden work, not isolated engine compute. Public model configuration fingerprints distinguish requested/reported/unknown settings without storing connection URLs. Historical `browser-1` files remain readable and may include estimated throughput; compare their protocol/provenance separately.

Results are stored in browser storage and can be downloaded or imported as JSON. Storage can be cleared or unavailable; if a storage warning appears, download the in-memory results before closing the page. Closing or reloading the page stops the browser benchmark, and a previously running result is shown as interrupted. On timeout the browser aborts its requests and stops the run, but cannot verify that the provider stopped inference or unload its model. Check the provider before starting another workload. Helper benchmarks instead continue in the local server when the page closes; see [measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md).

Results also shows a read-only shared catalog without requiring an endpoint connection. Hiding a shared result affects only this browser. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) to contribute a benchmark.

## Shared-results data boundary

The hosted site opens the shared Results library by default. Browsing it reads only the same-origin GitHub Pages catalog and benchmark JSON; it does not query desktop helper APIs or local files. Shared records identify their GitHub source. The published JSON omits host-local diagnostic text and paths while preserving measurements, failure classifications, hardware descriptions, settings and session provenance. It is a public projection of the repository record.

If the browser data client fails to load, the hosted site reports that failure rather than falling back to desktop APIs. Model-server access belongs to the optional Run workflow and starts only after an explicit Connect action.

The **Capabilities** library reads same-origin shared capability files, verifies their catalog SHA-256 and supports export/comparison. Dataset/score validation occurs during publication with the helper's deterministic re-scoring and fingerprint checks. The hosted page cannot launch capability tests or import unvalidated capability files; use the helper for those actions. Throughput JSON import remains available in browser Results. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

---

## docs/sharing-results.md

Canonical source: [docs/sharing-results.md](docs/sharing-results.md)

# Sharing and continuing benchmark results

The hosted Results view includes a shared catalog built from benchmark JSON files in this repository, alongside results stored in your browser. You can browse shared results without connecting a model provider or entering an API key. Shared entries are read-only; deleting one in the hosted view hides it in that browser and does not delete it from GitHub. Local browser results can be renamed and deleted locally.

## Contribute a benchmark

1. Run a benchmark using the [full helper](docs/getting-started.md) or [browser mode](docs/browser.md). Partial sessions and failures are useful contributions too.
2. In Results, download the benchmark's **JSON**. Review hardware information and all free text, including notes, model names, labels, reproduction fields and compute sources. Public outputs exclude endpoint URLs, credentials and credential environment-variable names; that filtering cannot decide whether your annotations are confidential. Browser results identify their separate client-timed protocol; helper results include sensor/session settings.
3. Sign in to GitHub and open [upload files to results/runs](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/upload/main/results/runs). Upload the single JSON file, named after its `id` with a `.json` extension. If you do not have write access, follow GitHub's fork prompt and propose the change from your fork.
4. Open the proposed pull request. The repository's validation checks run on the contribution. Once merged and the site deployment completes, the shared catalog updates automatically.

For a command-line contribution, fork and clone the repository, create a branch, and copy the single result file to `results/runs/`. Run `python tools/validate_results.py results/runs/<id>.json`, then `git add results/runs/<id>.json`, commit, push your branch and open a pull request. Stage the specific result file so unrelated local files and deletions are excluded.

## Add missing tests later

Same-file continuation applies to managed LM Studio runs. Generic endpoint and browser experiments require a new run; connection details are not stored in public result files.

A benchmark does not need every planned case before you contribute it. To complete or extend a managed LM Studio benchmark later, download its JSON and put it in the local helper's `results/runs/` directory using its `id` as the filename. In Results select it and choose **Add / rerun tests**. Existing models are preselected; select the models, sizes and query counts you want, review the preview, and choose **Add missing tests**. Existing terminal cases are preserved. Increase **Total repeats per test** to append repeats. To replace one specific measurement, choose its entry in **Tests to update**; previous attempts remain in history. Select **Retry failed tests** explicitly if you also want to retry failures and skipped cases.

The helper checks hardware, selected GPU and driver, corpus and LM Studio version for compatibility. Start a separate benchmark when those differ or cannot be verified. The same file records the added session and the helper saves a backup before modifying it. To update a contribution, submit the updated file with the same ID in a pull request; the saved cases travel with it. Do not manually edit measurements or replace failures with zeroes.

Browser mode can import and display JSON but cannot continue an existing benchmark. Its provider controls model execution and context. See [measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md) for retry, replacement and comparison rules.

## Reproducibility metadata

Hardware inventory describes the benchmark client. For remote inference, the result retains client inventory separately and does not claim it describes the server. Include public engine/version, model revision, quantization, actual context/KV settings, MTP draft count and runtime placement when known. Optional reproduction fields are marked `user_reported`; they do not configure the engine.

Only add compute claims with a source, arithmetic precision, execution path, dense/sparse distinction and peak/measured/estimate classification. INT precision uses TOPS; floating precision uses TFLOP/s. A claim is not a Wattever measurement. PCIe encoding ceilings are not measured DMA bandwidth, and idle link state can differ from loaded state. Compare client timings, provider timings and cache usage using their separate provenance; unknown cache usage is not zero. See [measurement definitions](docs/measurements.md).

## Capability results

Use **Capabilities → Export JSON** for one or more capability runs. These use `benchmark_kind: capability`, their own schema 1 and `results/capabilities/<id>.json`; keep throughput files in `results/runs/`. A `capability_runs` bundle is convenient for helper import/export; contribute individual run files under their IDs. The hosted catalog supports browsing/export/comparison; tests and validated imports require the helper. The hosted site does not write to GitHub.

Review generated visible answers, prompts, expected answers and source citations, as well as labels/notes and reported settings. Public audit material preserves exact content for dataset/protocol fingerprints and independent rescoring. Privacy-redacted responses are marked and cannot be re-imported as full, independently scored audit answers. Keep a reviewed original if needed.

Import re-scores answers and checks configuration/suite/protocol/subset fingerprints. These establish consistency, not authentication or proof that a model ran. Compare matching evaluation keys with scored/error/truncation counts and requested/reported/unknown effective settings. Automatically resolved opaque IDs and display names identify routes without sharing or hashing connection URLs. Keep the private helper/browser URL-to-ID registry out of contributions. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

---

## docs/measurements.md

Canonical source: [docs/measurements.md](docs/measurements.md)

﻿# Measurements and sessions

The local helper supports managed LM Studio and generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Hosted browser mode uses a separate `browser-2` protocol; historical `browser-1` files remain readable. Browser/helper timings and historical estimates are not directly interchangeable. See [Browser mode](docs/browser.md).

## Throughput and timing

A case combines a model, technique, prompt size, simultaneous query count and repeat. Successful, failed and skipped cases are recorded; inability to load or fit a workload is useful capacity information. Managed LM Studio can schedule Standard/MTP modes when a supported bundled MTP head exists, and disables reasoning by default. Generic endpoint technique, reasoning, context allocation, KV cache and quantization are controlled by the inference engine. Their effective state is unknown unless documented separately by the operator; a scheduler technique label does not prove the server's MTP state.

`prefill_tps` is prompt tokens divided by client-observed time to first output (TTFT). It includes queueing, network, tokenization and any unobserved reasoning before streamed content arrives. It is not an isolated engine prefill compute measurement. Decode throughput uses output tokens attributable to the observed stream interval, excluding its first-token estimate, divided by that client interval through stream completion. A stream chunk can contain multiple tokens. Generic endpoint throughput remains unavailable when server usage counts are missing; it is not estimated by counting chunks. Legacy managed results may carry explicitly marked chunk-based estimates. Inspect `metric_sources` and estimated-token flags.

`timing_scope` records whether first output is content or reasoning, the output kinds observed, empty deltas before output, reasoning-token provenance and the decode token scope. `decode_token_count` records the numerator actually used. Reported hidden reasoning tokens are excluded from decode when they were not streamed. When empty pre-output deltas suggest hidden reasoning and its token count is unknown, decode throughput remains unavailable. Even without that signal, an endpoint that does not report reasoning may leave hidden work unverified. Compare equivalent timing boundaries rather than assuming completion usage always measures visible text. Decode energy per token uses the same scoped numerator.

A response with only one observable output event has no observed interval between output events; decode speed remains unavailable rather than timing the trailing usage message. Optional `endpoint_reasoning_effort` records a requested standard API control; it does not certify that the engine obeyed it.

Provider-reported engine counters, when supplied, are stored separately in `reported_timings`; do not combine them with client timings. `cached_prompt_tokens` records provider usage detail when available. Missing cache usage means unknown, not zero. A unique leading nonce reduces ordinary prefix reuse but does not prove that all provider caching, routing or warm state has been controlled. Record cache policy and compare equivalent conditions.

Group throughput for concurrent requests includes prefill and queueing and differs from per-request decode speed. `aggregate_completion_tps` divides successful requests' total output tokens by group wall time; it is not the sum of decode speeds. Concurrent requests have overlapping phases, so group power does not get an invented prefill/decode energy split. Compare matching model builds, settings, corpus, measurement source and protocol.

## Context and workload

For managed LM Studio, the default per-test allocation reserves prompt tokens, output budget, 512 tokens of headroom and a 5% prompt safety margin, subject to the model's per-request maximum. Shared KV allocation multiplies per-request capacity by concurrency. The per-test policy reloads for each context/concurrency allocation; the optional fixed policy uses the largest planned allocation per model and MTP mode, reducing reloads while changing memory conditions. Generic endpoint context estimates describe client workload planning only; configure the real context/KV allocation in the engine. More concurrency consumes more memory; large contexts can fail to fit.

Prompt presets are 512, 5k, 10k, 20k, 40k, 80k, 100k, 120k, 150k, 200k and 260k tokens; concurrency presets are 1 through 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75 and 100. Compare cases at matching dimensions, output budget and repeat count. Close competing workloads and record relevant clock/power settings and runtime placement.

## Hardware, power and provenance

NVIDIA telemetry uses `nvidia-smi` for the selected card's board power. macOS may use `powermetrics` for GPU and CPU rails with permission. These have different boundaries. Whole-system power is estimated, not a meter reading, and includes only the selected GPU sensor. Selecting a sensor does not select inference placement. Generic endpoint power is unavailable unless `endpoint_inference_local: true` explicitly asserts that inference runs on the benchmark client. An externally loaded model prevents a verified unloaded-model idle baseline. Missing sensor data remains unavailable.

Hardware inventory is a best-effort, read-only snapshot of the benchmark client, not verified remote server hardware. Additive `metadata_schema_version: 1` metadata accompanies result `schema_version: 2`; historical files remain readable. Available fields include CPU/socket/core counts, RAM modules and reported clocks, GPU VRAM/driver, and current/max-reported PCIe generation and width. DIMM count does not establish active channels. PCIe snapshots can downshift while idle; reported maxima may reflect platform limits. `link_encoding_ceiling_bytes_per_second` is a derived one-direction ceiling after encoding only, excluding packet/system overhead. It is neither a measured DMA rate nor device-memory bandwidth. Unmeasured bandwidth remains null.

Helper throughput and capability benchmarks also run separate transfer microbenchmarks before inference. **Measure transfer bandwidth** in the machine panel runs them independently. Choose **Storage test folder** on the drive holding your weights, or leave it blank to test the results volume; the folder path is excluded from saved public configuration. Storage → RAM reads a flushed 256 MiB temporary file three times in 8 MiB blocks at queue depth one, bypassing the OS page cache with Windows unbuffered I/O, Linux `O_DIRECT` or macOS `F_NOCACHE`. Device/controller caches may still contribute. File creation is excluded from read timing, and the temporary file is removed. This is sequential read throughput on the selected filesystem, not random expert-fetch performance or a measurement of other drives.

RAM → VRAM uses the selected NVIDIA adapter, mapped by PCI bus, through the CUDA driver. It times completed copies from a 64 MiB pinned host buffer, with warmup, three 2 GiB samples, synchronization and a readback check. It describes host-to-device transfers, not internal VRAM bandwidth or pageable-memory performance. The probe avoids starting when reported free VRAM is below 512 MiB. Unsupported hardware, insufficient resources and failed probes are recorded as unavailable rather than estimated. No inference models are loaded or unloaded by the probes. An isolated worker has a 75-second limit.

`hardware.transfer_bandwidth` records protocol `wattever-transfer-v1`, capture time, scope, method, raw byte/time samples and their median bytes/second; UI rates use decimal MB/s and GB/s. Throughput execution sessions retain their own profile. Generic remote endpoints characterize the benchmark client, not the inference server. Browser-only mode cannot perform these native probes. A later measurement can be attached to a saved benchmark only on matching hardware and GPU/driver; it is marked `measured_later_on_matching_hardware`, with historical inference conditions unverified. Original inference measurements and session metadata are preserved.

Optional `reproducibility` settings and `performance_claims` are user-reported public annotations kept separate from detected fields. Record engine/version, model revision, quantization, context, KV precision and MTP draft count when known, plus placement and competing workloads in reviewed notes. Wattever does not invent TFLOPS from GPU names or model quantization. A sourced compute claim must state arithmetic precision, execution path, dense/sparse behavior and whether it is an advertised peak, independent measurement or estimate. Integer INT4/INT8 claims use TOPS; floating-point FP4/FP8/FP16/BF16/FP32 claims use TFLOP/s. Quantized weight storage does not establish inference arithmetic precision.

Quantization storage format (`quantization`, such as `Q4_0`) is separate from the method (`quantization_method`, such as QAT, QAD or UD). LM Studio discovery combines its model catalog and display labels, and records `quantization_source` and `quantization_method_source`. Unknown methods stay unknown; a four-bit format alone does not establish QAT or post-training quantization. Results and model selection show both labels when available. Historical catalog annotations use `lmstudio_catalog_backfill`, which does not verify historical weight bytes.

Each result can also carry a public `model_configuration` and `configuration_id`. It distinguishes requested model alias, canonical checkpoint, automatically resolved opaque endpoint ID/display name, operator reports and control-plane evidence. Endpoint naming provenance is detected, inferred, operator override or unknown; it is not established by ports or model aliases. The private URL-to-ID registry is excluded from public outputs, and URLs are not hashed into route IDs. Unknown quantization, reasoning or MTP is explicit. A configuration hash verifies consistency of public fields; it does not verify endpoint weights, effective settings or inference location. Historical user-reported endpoint identities remain readable. Capability task accuracy uses a separate protocol/result family; see [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

## Live telemetry and sustained observations

The helper samples whole-client CPU utilization and physical RAM usage independently of GPU sensor availability. GPU utilization, used VRAM, temperature, SM clock and board power describe the selected GPU. These measurements include competing processes and monitoring overhead; they do not isolate inference. VRAM percentage uses the selected adapter's reported capacity. Windows CPU temperature remains unavailable without an actual supported source; Linux may expose a CPU package sensor. Missing temperatures remain null, including on macOS without an available temperature source.

RAM usage means physical total minus OS-reported available memory on Windows and Linux. macOS uses total minus free/inactive pages and labels that availability boundary as an estimate. CPU utilization uses host CPU-time deltas, not load average. GPU snapshots are held briefly while fresh; failed/stale sensors do not become zero utilization.

Stored `telemetry.history` contains elapsed seconds, UTC timestamps, scope and up to 3,600 recent points with explicit ring-retention counts. At 150 ms this covers roughly nine minutes; older points can be dropped. `telemetry.summary` preserves all-run observed sample means, time-weighted means, maxima, first/last readings and coverage despite history eviction. Raw phase samples retain up to 72,000 rows; a phase older than that retention is flagged incomplete.

Time-weighted coverage excludes long sampling gaps. Peaks are observed maxima and can miss shorter spikes. Early/late 60-second means can overlap on short runs. Changes in temperature, clocks or load describe the observed workload/environment; they do not establish throttling or prove sustained model throughput. Compare repeat throughput at matching workload and placement alongside thermal/load traces. Separate graphs per selected metric avoid sharing incompatible units on one chart.

## Sessions and recovery

Each benchmark has one JSON file in `results/runs/`. Generic endpoints require reconnection and a new run rather than resume or same-file extension. A timeout stops the generic run because Wattever cannot verify provider-side cancellation or unload. Inspect the engine before restarting.

Managed LM Studio supports **Add / rerun tests**. Select models and Standard/MTP modes, prompt sizes and query counts, then review the preview. Increase **Total repeats per test** to append repeat slots without replacing saved measurements. Set **Timeout per test** for new attempts, including individual repairs; each session and result retains its actual budget. In **Tests to update**, choose one saved model/size/query-count/repeat to repair only that test; the All measurements table also provides a **Repair repeat** button. **Add missing tests** preserves terminal cases; **Retry failed tests** includes failures and skips; **Rerun selected tests** includes successful cases. A replaced attempt moves to `previous_attempts` and is not averaged with its replacement. An exact snapshot is kept in `results/.history/`. Each execution has session settings and provenance. Resume creates a new run for unfinished work. Both require compatible hardware, selected GPU/driver, corpus and LM Studio version; otherwise start a new benchmark.

Managed requests receive the configured per-test timeout. Prefill speed at shorter contexts does not shorten the budget for a larger context. The same whole-test budget applies while waiting for first output and during decode; output pauses do not impose a shorter hidden deadline. A timeout is a time limit, not physical freeze detection. The helper verifies managed model unload and worker exit before continuing; if verification fails, the run stops. Capacity failures can skip larger cases for that model/concurrency. By default, timeouts and transient request errors do not suppress subsequent repeats or larger contexts; a timed-out managed model is reloaded before another repeat. In the extension dialog's **Failure policy**, you can disable CPU placement fallback and opt to skip remaining repeats and larger contexts after a timeout. This records a practical time limit and explicit skips; it does not establish a hard VRAM allocation limit.

Older schemas and planner settings remain readable. An extended legacy run can contain sessions with different context planning; compare session settings rather than treating them as identical. See [API](docs/api.md), [FAQ](docs/faq.md), and [results guidance](results/README.md).

---

## docs/capabilities.md

Canonical source: [docs/capabilities.md](docs/capabilities.md)

# Capability evaluation

New question subsets use versioned SHA256 ranking of the selection seed and stable item IDs, independent of Python's sampling implementation. Historical Python-sampling records remain readable. Each run also records the exact selected IDs and their digest.

Use **Capabilities** to compare rule-scored task accuracy separately from throughput and power. Connect an endpoint in **Run**, then choose a model, suite, question count, seed, repeats and generation budget. Its display name and opaque route identity are supplied automatically. Launching tests and validating capability imports require the local Python helper. The hosted site can browse, export and compare shared capability results; it does not launch capability inference or import unvalidated capability files.

## Bundled suites

| Suite ID | Questions | Evaluation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `wattever-core-v1` | 24 | Original arithmetic, logic, typed JSON, instruction, retrieval and code-output tasks; four per category |
| `gsm8k-test-chat-v1` | 1,319 | GSM8K test split; zero-shot chat with final numeric-answer matching |
| `arc-challenge-test-chat-v1` | 1,172 | ARC-Challenge test split; zero-shot chat with generated answer-letter matching |

The external test splits are bundled for offline use. GSM8K is pinned to upstream revision `3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c` under MIT. ARC uses the `ARC-V1-Feb2018` archive's Challenge test member under CC BY-SA 4.0. The loader checks each extracted file's exact SHA-256 and item count before registering a suite. Source links, hashes, archive member, attribution and licenses are in [dataset provenance](corpora/capabilities/README.md). The archive ETag records source provenance; it is not the extracted file's cryptographic checksum.

**AI2 ARC-Challenge** contains grade-school multiple-choice science questions. It is distinct from the [ARC-AGI grid-reasoning benchmark](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi/1). The dashboard identifies its task type explicitly. A high score on this science-question suite is not an ARC-AGI score or a general intelligence rating. See the [AI2 dataset description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc).

These are versioned Wattever chat adaptations. GSM8K uses a zero-shot final `#### <number>` answer rather than a published few-shot harness. ARC normalizes option labels to letters and grades generated `ANSWER: <letter>` output rather than option likelihoods. Different prompts, sampling, item selections, output budgets and graders can change results. Do not equate these scores with official leaderboard or other harness scores. Public tasks may have appeared in training; none of these suites measures IQ or establishes a general intelligence ranking. Core is a small functional probe with a possible ceiling effect.

## Run and compare

1. Start the inference engine and load the intended model. Connect it in **Run**; no manual endpoint ID or label is needed. Use an optional canonical model ID if its served alias is ambiguous. An advanced **Display name** override can clarify an ambiguous detected name; keep it public and free of connection URLs or credentials.
2. Record quantization, model revision, engine/version, context/KV settings, reported reasoning and MTP where known. Configure actual settings in the engine. An omitted or unknown field does not mean disabled.
3. Open **Capabilities**, select the model and suite, and choose a subset or **Full suite**. The seed selects a deterministic subset; its exact IDs and digest are recorded. Use the same selection and evaluation settings across comparisons. Full suites can take substantial time and provider usage.
4. Review total generation tokens, optional deadline and repeats. Capability generation settings are independent of the speed benchmark. The default budget is 32,768 tokens for thinking plus final output, with no wall-clock deadline (`0`). This is a ceiling, not a request to generate that many tokens. The server's loaded context and provider limits can impose lower limits. Use Stop to cancel, or set an explicit item deadline when needed. The UI defaults requested reasoning to **None**; **Provider default** omits that API field. Unsupported reasoning requests fail visibly. A short total budget can truncate reasoning before a final answer appears. Inspect the observed reasoning, token usage, output-limit count and coverage; a requested reasoning setting does not prove the engine honored it. Keep budgets consistent across comparable configurations and report deliberate budget changes as separate evaluations.
5. Start the test. One request runs at a time, with a fresh chat per item/repeat. No model load/unload or MTP command is sent. Local CPU/RAM/GPU telemetry is available only after explicitly confirming inference runs on this computer, including when using an LM Studio endpoint.
6. Open a saved result to explore its dashboard. Select category bars, outcomes or repeats to filter the question matrix, then select a cell to inspect the prompt, expected output and visible response. Select multiple results for configuration comparisons. Different evaluation keys indicate different experiments.

Requested sampling is recorded, including temperature, optional top-p and reasoning effort. The seed always determines question selection. **Also send seed to the inference API** is off by default; with `send_seed: true`, it additionally requests `seed + repeat` for generation. Top-p defaults to omitted, and a blank temperature omits that parameter. The endpoint's determinism and effective settings are not independently verified. Repeats expose response variation on the same questions and do not create independent new questions. A provider can change its served weights or routing without changing its public alias; record any known changes as a new configuration.

## Explore a result

The overview keeps score and coverage together. Its header shows selected questions versus total suite questions, repeat count, and the descriptive first-repeat 95% interval when recorded. Subset scores are labeled as subsets; a 50-question sample is not the full 1,172-question ARC-Challenge test split. Small samples and scores near the ceiling can limit the ability to distinguish configurations; inspect the questions, coverage and paired evidence rather than comparing headline percentages alone.

The dashboard includes:

| View | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Strict rule pass rate** | Passed attempts divided by graded attempts; request errors are excluded |
| **Correct / planned** | Passed attempts divided by every planned attempt, including unfinished work |
| **Evaluation coverage** | Graded attempts divided by planned attempts |
| **Issues to review** | Rule mismatches, output limits and request errors, with distinct outcomes |
| **Capability profile** | Category pass rates with passed/graded and graded/planned counts |
| **Outcome breakdown** | A ring and legend separating passes, rule mismatches, output limits, request errors, cancellation, ungraded and unrecorded attempts |
| **Consistency across repeats** | Per-repeat pass rates and questions whose recorded pass/fail outcome changed |

Select a chart segment, category bar or repeat point to filter the **Question explorer**. Combine category, outcome, repeat and text filters; **Clear filters** restores the full selection. The matrix places questions in rows and repeats in columns, with 12 questions per page. Symbols and outcome labels accompany colors. Unrecorded cells are visible rather than counted as failures.

Select a cell to open its evidence inspector. The question appears above expected and actual output, followed by a human-readable explanation of the recorded rule. Copy controls and previous/next navigation help review matching attempts. **Grading evidence & request metadata** contains the raw grading, normalization, usage and timing fields in a collapsed panel. Model responses remain inert text; inspecting them executes no generated code.

An exact-rule mismatch can be a format failure. For example, if the task requires only `528`, the response `The answer is 528.` fails the exact-text rule despite containing the expected number. Inspect the required output and grading explanation before concluding that the model failed the arithmetic. The dashboard presents the recorded decision; it does not relax the rule or add a model judge.

Live results update as attempts finish while preserving question filters and input focus. You can inspect another saved result without being redirected to the active run. Older files that contain only aggregate scores are labeled **Reported summary only**; question evidence is not reconstructed from their totals.

For API clients, fetch the full run and its suite manifest once through `/api/capabilities/runs/<id>`, then consume `/api/capabilities/events?cursor=<cursor>`. Apply result updates by item ID and repeat, retain the returned cursor, and refresh the final saved result after completion. This avoids repeatedly transferring the full question manifest. See the [API reference](docs/api.md) for request and event routes.

## Compare configurations

Select results in the library and choose a baseline. Overall and category bars show recorded pass rates with their graded denominators. A paired change is available only when evaluation fingerprints and declared suite, scoring, selected questions, sampling and answer-budget settings match. Otherwise the bars remain descriptive and the dashboard marks the paired result **Not comparable**.

The paired percentage-point change is the compared result minus the baseline, using only matching item-ID/repeat pairs graded in both runs. Wins, losses and ties describe those same scored pairs. Errors, cancelled requests, ungraded records and missing observations do not become losses. Different repeat counts can leave unmatched observations outside the paired calculation. This paired change can differ from subtracting overall pass rates when the runs have different graded coverage.

Repeat variation means that scored pass/fail flags changed for the same question. A request error followed by a pass is an availability difference, not evidence of answer variation. The dashboard introduces no new scoring protocol or independence assumption; use the statistical context below when interpreting gaps.

## Grading and uncertainty

Scorers are deterministic and auditable. Exact text ignores surrounding whitespace. Typed JSON rejects duplicate keys, non-finite values, extra keys and value/type mismatches. Numeric final answers use decimal comparison with validated number formatting. Multiple-choice scoring checks the final answer label. No model judge or generated-code execution is used.

Only visible final-answer content is scored; streamed reasoning is not treated as the final answer. A successfully completed stream retains its finish reason, usage and observation metadata even when no final answer appears. Empty final output at `finish_reason: "length"` is an output-limit failure; empty final output at normal completion is a failed task answer. Neither is a transport error. `finish_reason: "length"` is scored incorrect even when a partial answer resembles the expected result. Transport errors and cancellation are unscored and counted separately. A configured positive request deadline stops the evaluation; the helper cannot verify provider-side cancellation. It blocks another benchmark while its request worker remains active. Inspect the engine before restarting.

`accuracy` and `percent` divide correct answers by scored observations, excluding unscored errors. Always inspect `planned`, `attempts`, `scored`, `errors`, `cancelled` and `truncated`. `penalized_accuracy` divides correct answers by all planned observations; unfinished work reduces it. Category and per-repeat statistics accompany the total.

The 95% Wilson interval uses distinct scored items from the first repeat only. It is a descriptive binomial approximation: questions may be correlated and are not a representative sample of intelligence. Repeated responses are dependent observations. An interval is not a significance test between models, and overlapping or non-overlapping intervals alone do not establish a ranking. Compare matching suite/subset, scoring version, token budget and sampling settings, with coverage and failure rates visible.

## Configuration identity and result files

New evaluations record completion policy `finished-stream-visible-answer-v2` in their evaluation fingerprint. Historical no-final-answer error records can lack finish reasons and usage; their cause cannot be reconstructed from the stored record. They remain unchanged and carry an interpretation notice in the dashboard. Rerun with adequate generation settings for a complete evaluation.

Each result contains `model_configuration` and its SHA-256 `configuration_id`. The public configuration records requested/canonical model identifiers, public endpoint ID/label/provider, quantization, engine/version, model revision/source, context/KV settings, and requested/reported/effective reasoning and MTP. Unknown values stay explicit. Effective settings require control-plane evidence; accepting a request is not that evidence. Endpoint URLs and credentials do not enter this public fingerprint.

Connect or a direct start supplies endpoint identity automatically. Naming provenance distinguishes detected service metadata, inference from an official cloud host/declared managed provider, an optional operator display-name override and unknown software. Ports and model aliases are not software evidence. An unknown provider keeps a generic location-based name rather than a guessed engine. Canonical known public API routes use stable public provider IDs; other routes use privately generated opaque IDs with URL mappings kept in the ignored helper registry or browser local storage. Route origin and provider branding do not verify inference location or backend weights, and historical user-reported identities remain readable. See [automatic endpoint identity](docs/api.md#automatic-endpoint-identity).

The suite has a version and content digest. `evaluation_key` fingerprints the evaluation protocol and selected items; repeat count is recorded separately. Fingerprints establish content consistency, not authentication, proof that inference happened, or proof of which weights an endpoint served.

Capability files use `benchmark_kind: "capability"`, `schema_version: 1`, and a separate `results/capabilities/<id>.json` directory. They include the public suite, item answers, scorer decisions, usage/timing provenance and summary. Throughput files remain in `results/runs/` with their existing schema. See [API](docs/api.md) for read/start/cancel/import/export routes.

Import accepts one capability run or an object containing `capability_runs`. It validates public configuration/suite/protocol fingerprints, deterministic item selection and observation uniqueness, then independently re-scores visible audit answers and recomputes statistics. A completed result requires all planned observations. A response redacted for privacy cannot be independently re-scored and is rejected as a full audit import. Preserve the reviewed original locally if you need that audit.

Public suite prompts, expected answers and source citations must remain exact for their digest and audit. Review them, generated answers and all annotations before sharing. Connection credentials and URLs are excluded as connection metadata; arbitrary task text can still contain information you do not want to publish. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) and [security](SECURITY.md).

---

## docs/architecture.md

Canonical source: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md)

# Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    UI[Local browser UI] -->|HTTP on loopback| Server[Wattever server]
    Server --> Runner[Benchmark runner]
    Server --> Cap[Capability runner]
    Cap -->|Sequential streaming requests| Endpoint
    Cap --> Suites[Offline pinned suites and deterministic scorers]
    Cap --> CapStore[Capability JSON and audit answers]
    Cap --> Sensors
    Runner --> Identity[Public model configuration identity]
    Cap --> Identity
    Runner -->|CLI and streaming API| LMS[LM Studio]
    Runner -->|Streaming Chat Completions| Endpoint[Externally managed endpoint]
    Server -->|Optional model discovery| Endpoint
    Runner --> Corpus[Local prompt corpus]
    Runner --> Sensors[GPU and system telemetry]
    Runner --> Store[JSON results and history]
    Server --> Store
    Server --> UI
    Hosted[Hosted browser UI] --> Adapter[Browser adapter]
    Adapter -->|OpenAI-compatible API| Provider[Model provider]
    Adapter --> BrowserStore[Browser storage and JSON export]
```

The standard-library server serves local static assets and coordinates one benchmark at a time. The runner plans cases, collects streaming responses and optional power samples, and saves progress to JSON. Managed LM Studio uses its CLI for model lifecycle and context/MTP scheduling. The generic endpoint adapter sends streaming Chat Completions requests and optionally discovers model IDs; the engine manages model lifecycle and execution settings. Both use the same helper workload and result pipeline. The UI reads status and events and displays saved results.

Discovery inventories the benchmark client using bounded OS/driver probes. It does not establish remote inference hardware. Generic local-power attribution requires an explicit user assertion. Detected fields, user-reported reproduction settings, sourced compute claims, provider timings and client timings remain distinct. Public result projection removes endpoint connection details and credentials; free-text fields still require review. Result files preserve case/session provenance, and older schema 2 files remain readable with additive metadata. See [measurements](docs/measurements.md), [API](docs/api.md), and [getting started](docs/getting-started.md).

Connect/direct starts resolve endpoint identity without required naming fields. Explicit service metadata and known public API hosts establish detected/inferred service labels; unsupported discovery keeps generic names. Canonical public API routes use stable provider IDs, while other routes use private URL-to-random-ID mappings. Port numbers and model aliases are not software evidence. Route identity and inference-local attribution remain separate.

The hosted browser adapter connects directly to the configured provider after the user chooses Connect. It has no hosted proxy or helper credentials and cannot access helper telemetry or control model loading. The browser and helper use different measurement protocols; see [browser mode](docs/browser.md).

The capability runner shares transport and public model identity with throughput runs but uses separate protocols, storage and deterministic grading. Bundled dataset files are checked against pinned checksums before suite registration; no dataset download occurs during evaluation. One speed or capability benchmark runs at a time. Timeout/cancellation prevents subsequent work while a request worker remains active because provider-side termination is unverified. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

Telemetry has an independent host CPU/RAM sampler and a streaming GPU reader. Recent history is bounded; online all-run aggregates preserve observed means/peaks and coverage. Neither hardware discovery nor telemetry establishes remote inference hardware. The hosted result catalog is read-only and can expose both result families without provider access; launching capability tests requires the helper.
